EIC Teens 2 · Unit 6 walkthrough

Before you plan today's class

One unit, five lessons, plan each one on its own

This unit isn't one lesson, it's five: 6a, 6b, 6c, 6d, and 6e. Even a single lettered section can spill across two classes, and that's normal. The lead-in, guided practice, and free production cycle happens every class, not once for the whole chapter.

1 · Start

Where does today pick up? Maybe reviewing yesterday's homework is your warm-up.

2 · Land

Where do you want to stop today? You don't have to reach free production every class, but decide on purpose, don't just run out of time.

3 · Homework

Whatever's left over becomes homework, and that homework becomes tomorrow's warm-up.

"I'm not just the middle step, I'm the loop. What doesn't finish today, I carry into tomorrow's warm-up." · Flow

Used once, on day 1 of the unit: it sets up the theme for everything that follows.

6a is its own lesson, and it alone may take more than one class. Decide where you'll stop.

A separate lesson from 6a: bring its own lead-in, don't assume the unit-opener photo still counts.

Another full lesson on its own, reading-heavy, so pace the two reads deliberately.

6d and 6e are two separate lessons sharing a spread: treat them as two different class plans.

Spark says
The photo

Cover the caption before you show this. Ask: "Who are these people? When do you think they lived?" Let students argue for a guess before anyone's right or wrong.

Day 1 · Unit lead-in

Exercise 1

Pairs talk before you confirm anything. Don't reveal answers yet: the guessing is the activity, not a step to rush through.

Exercise 5

This is where the unit stops being about history and becomes about them. Good place to end day 1, on their own family photos, not on a grammar point.

Day 1 · Unit lead-in

6a · Exercise 1

This is 6a's own lead-in, separate from the unit-opener photo used on day 1. Notes and coins from their own country make a fresh hook before the reading.

Lead-in for this lesson
Build says
Grammar · was/were

Don't explain this box out loud. Point at it and ask exercise 4's questions instead: let them find the rule in the examples that are already sitting right there.

Guided practice
Build says
Vocabulary · time expressions

Let them order these before you explain any of them. The ordering task IS the teaching moment, not a preliminary step before the real one.

Guided practice
Build says
Pronunciation · -ed endings

Play the audio before you explain the syllable rule. Let them hear it first, then confirm the pattern.

Guided practice
Dare says
Ex 12 · Speaking and Writing

If you don't reach this today, that's fine: it becomes tomorrow's warm-up, not something to rush the grammar to get to. But when you do run it: no grammar box to check, resist jumping in if they get stuck.

Free production · may need its own day
Spark says
6b · Exercise 1

New lesson, new lead-in. Which companies do they already know? This is a fresh hook, don't assume 6a's energy carries over automatically.

Lead-in for this lesson
Build says
Grammar · irregular verbs & negatives

Irregular verbs need recognition, not memorization on the spot. Point to the pattern examples first, then let exercise 4's questions do the explaining for you.

Guided practice
Build says
Grammar · past simple questions

This box builds directly on the negatives box next to it. If you're splitting 6b across two days, this is a natural place to pick back up.

Guided practice
Dare says
Interview your partner

Real questions about a real classmate, using everything from this lesson, with no script to fall back on. That's the point.

Free production · may need its own day
Spark says
"Sharing Your Past"

This portrait is 6c's own mini lead-in. Ask what they think "lifelogging" means before anyone reads a word of the article.

Lead-in for this lesson
Build says
Reading · matching paragraphs

First read, no dictionary, general idea only. Save the detail questions (exercise 4) for the second pass.

Guided practice
Build says
Word focus · "write"

Chunks, not words. "Write by hand" and "write in a notebook" get remembered together, not as isolated vocabulary.

Guided practice
Dare says
Prepare and run a survey

Writing their own questions, then actually interviewing other groups. This one has two parts, planning and doing, don't let planning eat the whole class.

Free production · may need its own day
Spark says
6d · Listening, first pass

First listen of a new lesson doubles as its lead-in: general idea only, no transcript, no translating line by line.

Lead-in for this lesson
Build says
Real life · asking what people did

This chart is a toolkit, not a text to read aloud. Have them build a few questions from it themselves before exercise 2.

Guided practice
Dare says
Exercise 5 · Pairs practice

No script this time, just their own last night, last weekend, own words. This is where 6d's whole lesson pays off.

Free production
Spark says
6e · Exercise 1

Do they ever actually write thank-you messages? This personal question is 6e's own lead-in, don't skip straight to the writing skill box.

Lead-in for this lesson
Build says
Writing skill · formal/informal

Have them sort the three real messages into formal vs informal first, then fill the chart. The pattern should come from the examples, not from you explaining it up front.

Guided practice
Dare says
Exercise 4 · Write your own

No sample message to copy from here, just a situation. This is where you find out if the formal/informal distinction actually stuck.
